Tech Report: You cannot replay missions in GTA 6, but you can use multiple save files, as Rockstar explains how it made missions "harder to fail"

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eurogamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that you cannot replay GTA 6 missions again once you've completed them.
  • Recent findings suggest that you can, of course, use the game's 15 save slots instead - but considering that there will be many, many more missions than there are slots, you're going to have to think about when and where you want to make a record of your progress.
  • Sources indicate that it seems, though, that it's going to be a bit harder than in previous games to hit that fail state in GTA 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you cannot replay GTA 6 missions again once you've completed them. This might be a shock to some people, since the option to do so was included in Rockstar games as recently as GTA 5, but here once you've made progress in the story, that's it. Our reviewer confirmed this in his 100+ hour playthrough of the title.

Recent findings suggest that you can, of course, use the game's 15 save slots instead - but considering that there will be many, many more missions than there are slots, you're going to have to think about when and where you want to make a record of your progress. By my maths, that means you're going to want to make a new manual save for every 6.6 percent of the game you complete. There is, of course, an auto-save slot, too, that should help you out if you get Busted or Wasted. There will also be key story missions - you will be able to tell when they are, much like you could tell when there was about to be a substantial heist in GTA 5, a showdown in GTA: San Andreas, or a raid on a gang lord's mansion in GTA: Vice City - that you may want to save before attempting.

Sources indicate that it seems, though, that it's going to be a bit harder than in previous games to hit that fail state in GTA 6. "The team embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project," notes David Hynd, vice president of technology on GTA 6. "For example, we really wanted to reduce the number of Mission fails for the player experimenting or trying something different. And we wanted to encourage the player to do what felt right to them for their particular play style.".

That means that Rockstar, by considering its deployment of standard gameplay mechanics and enemy AI, and re-evaluating how it approached mission and level design, has created "many different ways" for you to approach any given mission in the game. The result? "It's a lot harder to keep Missions as open as possible (especially in a game as large as this), but the freedom and flexibility it allows the player was worth it," says Hynd. He also notes that the team expects players to "learn and reapply" consistent rules in terms of how the world works - and be surprised when they do and don't apply.

Sources indicate that in the previous game, you could access any previous mission you'd completed and be able to play it again on a whim. For GTA 5, you'd simply boot up Story Mode, open the pause menu, go to Game > Replay Mission, and pick the mission you want to play. GTA 6's structure is more complicated, though, hence why Rockstar made the decision to make progress this linear.

If you want to, ahem, 'travel to Upcoming Zealand' to get ahead of the timezones, it seems the country would be happy to have you.

Industry observers note that this means you can kick off a playthrough as a lowborn leader of a travelling band or a wandering noble with claims on realms ruled by others. Originally locked behind the Roads to Power DLC, the option to start off this way or end up living if you end up deposed from your throne of choice is a great addition to the story arc of any CK3 run. No longer are you glued to the throne from day one to the day you quit for good - power's a privilege which can be earned and revoked depending on what you get up to. Though, it's worth noting that only three ways of operating as a landless adventurer are being made free to access with this revision. You can be an aimless wanderers, sword-toting mercenaries, or scholars. If you want your band to earn their living as explorers, free booters, or legitimists, you'll still need Roads to Power.

It has been revealed that each run revolves around flipping cards to generate money and multipliers while using hints to deduce the location of dangerous JERRY cards. Push your luck too far, and the run collapses.

Stack the deck in your favor, exploit strange synergies, and make your quota before closing time… or else.

Runs are short, decisions are risky, and every card flip is a calculated gamble as players climb the corporate ladder. The further they progress, the stranger the office becomes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you've been online at all today, you'll know that what feels like the entire world is presently fawning over GTA 6. As the reviews dropped, one thing promptly became very clear: this is a game absolutely packed with detail. Our own Chris noted that, thanks to this focus on specific detail and unbelievable nuance, Grand Theft Auto 6 is "the most unbelievable video game world ever made". And it's no accident: this is something Rockstar put a lot of dedicated effort into.

It's been well-established that the studio has gone above and beyond to make this interactive world one of the most richly-developed we've ever seen: Rockstar has told us it "re-engineered" its weather systems to "achieve a sense of scale we haven't felt before," adding hurricanes, rainbows and heavy rain. It simulated and built a complex drug system, allowing Lucia and Jason to partake in drug use "directly from their inventory" and "at any time". But there are still details emerging from the dev team that are blowing my mind. And the most recent byte of information I saw was related to how Rockstar worked with sound.

"Much of the dynamic soundscape is informed by the incredibly detailed art throughout the world," explains Alastair MacGregor, vice president of audio at Rockstar. "One small example is that convenience store refrigerators all have their own unique sounds. In a run-down store, the refrigerators and freezers are loud and sound like they are badly maintained. Their compressor units can be heard mechanically whirring away from years of neglect. As a result, the bottles behind the doors can be heard shaking and the units click on and off more frequently. In an up-market store, the refrigerators are quieter, adding a subtle hum to the environment.".

Industry observers note that this level of detail is, quite frankly, absurd. It's a testament to granularity Rockstar is willing to go to in making Leonida feel truly lived-in and realistic. And this level of production isn't restricted to internal locations, either. "On the ambient side, we love the contrast between the manicured luxury islands, with the sizzle of crickets and lawn sprinklers backed by birdsong, yacht halyards clanging in the distance, and yard work going on, versus urban areas with the sounds of people living on top of each other - snatches of every genre of music, distant voices, cars peeling out, construction, the omnipresent hum of elderly air conditioners struggling with the humidity," continues MacGregor.

He goes on to say that if you're wandering the streets of Gellhorn - a coastal city in Kelly County on the western side of Leonida - it's acoustically a very different vibe than the high-rise centre of Vice City, where the sound bounces between the buildings. This means that the engine is handling not just the sounds of things as minute as bugs in the grass, but also how that sound travels, and interacts with other physical entities in the world. "We've spent years iterating on reverb technology to make sure that you can feel that - from the pops of cars backfiring to the wash of a helicopter passing by overhead to birds squawking in the trees," concludes MacGregor.

It has been revealed that GTA 6 introduces tomorrow - Thursday, 19th November - for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It's also worth noting that Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week.

Recent findings suggest that I like to think I'm difficult to hypnotise, but I confess, I'm a sucker for those Youtube adverts for the mobile vertical shooters. You know the ones: boglins pour towards an auto-firing player, who must dodge about to grab upgrades while whittling down the horde. The player in the advert always does pretty well for 20 seconds, but ahhhh, then they get just a tiny bit overconfident, mistime how long it'll take them to erode the health of an ogre midboss, and: bam!

Sources indicate that show me one of those ads, and I'll always watch to the end in the hope that this time, the protagonist will Study The Blade, conquer their harmatia, and slay the damn ogre. I've never actually played any of the mobile shooters in question, mind you. I'm far too cultured for that, you dope! Except that I've just been playing the demo for Korridor, which is supposedly "based off" of the ads, but might as well be one of the games they're promoting, for all I know.

Per the Steam page, it claims to have turned the above advert format into a whole new "deeply strategic genre", the "gates shooter", by stirring in "elements of roguelikes and bullet heavens". I need somebody to authenticate whether this is a truthful statement, or developer TinyToad pulling a fast one. In the meantime, I'll say that 1) I have now managed to kill several ogres, 2) I like Korridor's electro-metal soundtrack.

According to recent reports, in Korridor, you're a bald medieval monk garbed in Poundshop Adeptus Astartes platemail. You've woken up in a dungeon of mysterious provenance, and must walk very slowly down its corridors korridors while shooting and punching goblins, wraiths and demons hurrying the other way. Each enemy has a numerical health indicator, and the basic challenge is working out whether you can empty it before they walk into you – which costs you a proportionate amount of health, mitigated by armour. As you go, you'll walk through a choice of gates that grant buffs such as faster health regen, bullet penetration, or nippier horizontal motion.

The fact that you don't control how fast the monk trudges vertically allows the game to synch the onslaught pretty tightly to the thudding, growling score. It reminds me a little of Thumper, though it isn't nearly so invigoratingly malevolent. So far. At intervals, the beat thickens and all the enemies burst into a sprint, throwing their arms up and conveying the strong impression that they are more running away from something than running at you. There's clearly a dreadful entity at the far end of the dungeon. Perhaps it is another overdressed monk with an even bigger gun.

According to recent reports, is this how those mobile games actually work? If it is, then alas and alack, all is lost. I've finally succumbed to those adverts, and all it took was some disingenuous Steam copy promising to place them at a critical remove. Curse you, TinyToad. Curse you and your gates. If you were actually a toad, I'd step on you. Still, now that we've broken the ice, can you please make another game in which I get to play one of those gloating giantesses in Hero Wars? Because I know some people who dig that kind of thing.

#63160. Latest Update: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1840 w)

Latest Update: World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1840 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rockpapershotgun

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I don't play video games regularly anymore.
  • Sources indicate that here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019.
  • Industry observers note that my relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a newly introduced legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Sources indicate that here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a latest Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

Industry observers note that my relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my latest parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. Newly introduced players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

According to recent reports, the persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

According to recent reports, the original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as significant as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

Recent findings suggest that I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an vital byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn newly introduced tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually rolled out Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When newly introduced content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

In a recent development, there are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

Recent findings suggest that as I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

Recent findings suggest that I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted aims designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

According to recent reports, many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each upcoming wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you're anything like me, you're planning on settling down to a long weekend of GTA 6.
  • It has been revealed that "There is so much to do in Leonida," Donkin said in development notes supplied to press.
  • Recent findings suggest that it's a bold ambition for players trained on at least a generation of games that do ask them to approach open worlds like a checklist, but Donkin has his reasons: "When you play the game and take your time with it, playing at the pace it asks you to, it can really unfold in front of you in a way that can feel almost infinite at a macro level, but each individual encounter still feels hand-crafted and with a human behind it," he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're anything like me, you're planning on settling down to a long weekend of GTA 6. But before you do, it might be worth hearing from Rockstar VP of design, Stephen Donkin, who states that Vice City represents a new kind of open world - one you shouldn't try and approach in the same way as a traditional game.

It has been revealed that "There is so much to do in Leonida," Donkin said in development notes supplied to press. "And so much to discover, that we hope players get to the point where they stop thinking in tasks, completion percentages, online guides, and rather let the game unfold in front of them.".

Recent findings suggest that it's a bold ambition for players trained on at least a generation of games that do ask them to approach open worlds like a checklist, but Donkin has his reasons: "When you play the game and take your time with it, playing at the pace it asks you to, it can really unfold in front of you in a way that can feel almost infinite at a macro level, but each individual encounter still feels hand-crafted and with a human behind it," he says. "If players can let go and submit to becoming immersed in the world of Leonida, and just follow their nose as they play, they will feel the Leonida I have felt - and that's all we could ask for.".

In a recent development, this is actually one of the things that's making me most excited to experience GTA 6. The depth of some of its systems make it sound more like an RPG or even an immersive sim than the traditional action games that the previous games in the series have been, and getting a chance to invest in those slowly strikes me as the thing that's likely to set GTA 6 the furthest apart from similar titles.

In a recent development, the type of game that doesn't direct you to its every corner in pursuit of some type of reward or checklist is few and far between, especially when you're talking about sprawling, open-world RPGs. The Witcher 3 and Breath of the Wild/Tears of the Kingdom come to mind, the latter in particular far more interested in getting you to play around with its tools than simply achieving set goals. But certainly there's been a trend of open world games that do the opposite - Assassin's Creed titles have long leaned towards completing tasks and collecting items. And in fact, Grand Theft Auto itself used to ask much more of the player in terms of collectibles and minigames if anyone wanted to attempt to 100% them. The likes of Vice City Stories and Liberty City Stories were much smaller games, but searching for red balloons and stray pigeons was something of a drag towards the end of the PS2 era. That GTA 6 is so deliberately shrugging that off is what could turn it into the next great open-world benchmark.

Recent findings suggest that the previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

The employment tribunal over Rockstar's firing of 34 workers last year has come to an end for now, pending a final verdict from the judge. Said judge hasn't offered a concrete estimate of when her judgement will arrive, but has reportedly asserted that she'll provide it "as promptly as [she] possibly can".

In a recent development, that's according to People Make Games' Chris Bratt, who's reported on the tribunal throughout the proceedings."I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case," he cited judge Lucy Wiseman as having mentioned following closing arguments from Rockstar and the union representing the fired staff over the past couple of days. "What I will say is that I will use my best [endeavours] to get that judgement out as promptly as I possibly can.".

Bratt reported that could mean anything from weeks to a few months of waiting, leaving the fired staff looking at more time in the limbo they've occupied throughout the tribunal.

Recent findings suggest that to recap the arguments Wiseman will have heard, Rockstar accused the fired staff of leaking "confidential information on a public forum", while the Independent Workers’ union of Great Britain (IWGB) union have accused Rockstar of being motivated by union busting in letting the workers go. According to a previous report from People Make Games, discussion of a new company Slack policy in a union-run Discord server preceded the firings.

The fired devs haven't called for supporters to boycott GTA 6 - the game they were working on prior to being let go - in solidarity, but instead to consider buying specially-designed union t-shirts, the proceeds of which will go towards the workers' "Fighting Fund".

Devs still at Rockstar and the IWGB have formed the Rockstar Games Workers Union since their fired colleagues' tribunal proceedings began and are in the midst of a vote on union recognition as of writing.

Recent findings suggest that writing in The Guardian's Comment Is Free section this week, Rockstar animation programmer Nestor Uriarte expressed that it's "hard not to worry about what the future holds" for developers at the studio, with the prospect of layoffs potentially happening now the substantial game is out the door concerning staff. Uriarte made clear that, as of the writing of his piece, Rockstar staff "have had no indication that layoffs are coming".

Latest Update: PC gamers notice Nvidia's drivers hammering their SSDs with tens of GB/hr of unnecessary writes – revert to 621.01 ASAP

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (573 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pcgamer

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, another day, another dodgy driver: Nvidia's latest driver package (621.24) is needlessly writing to customers' SSDs, in some cases by 30 GB every hour.
  • According to recent reports, the issue appears to be fairly widespread going from reports on the Nvidia GeForce forum, Dell forum, Super User forum, and many, many threads on Reddit.
  • According to recent reports, you can then see how much each process has written, which shouldn't usually be very much at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, another day, another dodgy driver: Nvidia's latest driver package (621.24) is needlessly writing to customers' SSDs, in some cases by 30 GB every hour. And if that sounds familiar, it's because an glitch with Radeon Adrenalin drivers did a similar thing a week ago.

According to recent reports, the issue appears to be fairly widespread going from reports on the Nvidia GeForce forum, Dell forum, Super User forum, and many, many threads on Reddit. Though that's a bunch of people that might, and did, notice random writes to their SSD; many more may not visit their task manager to check these things with any regularity.

According to recent reports, you can then see how much each process has written, which shouldn't usually be very much at all. I measured my own PC on an older driver version (621.01) and this process had only written 63 MB in an hour of uptime; if you're on the most recent GeForce driver package (621.24), and NVDisplay.Container.exe has a number of gigabytes next to it (it's in bytes, so get your calculator out), you've been bit by the bug.

The affected driver, 621.24, is still available to download right now. That's the surprising thing here, as the concern has seemingly been reported across the internet since November 15; the driver was released on November 12, and it appears to have taken a few days of needlessly huge writes for anyone to notice.

The culprit appears to be a binary log stored at 'C:\ProgramData\NVIDIA Corporation\nvtopps\nct\nvlog.nvlgstg'.

This log is being constantly rewritten, rather than appended to, according to the initial report by TroubleGrid. The large file is rewritten each time, therefore it keeps growing over a short period while a PC is switched on; the problem with multiplication like that is repeated multiplication leads to exponential growth. If those writes are sustained around the 1–2 MB/s mark, that's upwards of 5–7 GB/hr, though some users suggest it gets much worse.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products.

It has been revealed that the easiest fix is to revert to the previous driver, 621.01 (clean install option on Nvidia installer or use Display Driver Uninstaller first). There is another fix for anyone hoping to keep the latest Game Ready support, as posted by one user on Reddit and generated by Claude. That's a command that changes the Registry to prevent further writes, while retaining functionality of other Game Ready driver features.

What's most surprising here is that the driver is still live on Nvidia's site—it should've been pulled days ago.

According to recent reports, the love, joy and merriment of the holiday season are always infectious in theme parks. As part of Universal Epic Universe’s holiday celebration expansion for 2026, the decorations have been scaled up (sorry, I had to work a dragon reference in there) in How to Train Your Dragon – Isle of Berk for Snoggletog, and guests are all the better for it.

I got to experience the newborn theme park’s first holiday season in 2025, which was festive but also promised so much future possibility. Seeing what Universal was able to pull together just six months into the opening of their newest theme park just made me want more of everything. At that time, Snoggletog was relegated to a banner hung in the Isle of Berk gift shop that you could miss and never know it was there if you didn’t wander inside. So, I was particularly excited to learn that this year, the annual holiday inspired by modern Christmas traditions would be expanded throughout the land.

Sources indicate that for those not in the know, Snoggletog is the winter holiday celebrated by the Viking community on the fictional Isle of Berk in the How to Train Your Dragon franchise. It features feasts and festivities fit for dragons and even includes the seasonal Harvest Mac & Cheese Cone at Hooligan’s Grog & Gruel. And there’s now a row of trees, just inside the entrance, decorated with what looks to be homemade ornaments that are a fun detail to check out during the day and beautiful to look at once they’re lit up at night.

It has been revealed that epic Universe is already a significant award winner and popular destination with a ton of great attractions. I appreciate that they’re not wasting any time by expanding their offerings, too, even with something that seems as small as holiday decorations. (Not to mention there’s that construction on an Epic Universe expansion for an indoor coaster.).

While my own gothic heart remains in Darkmoor, through the Dark Universe portal, Isle of Berk feels like the most expansive and detailed area of Epic Universe, so it’s especially nice to see this holiday celebration get the extra attention it deserves. It’s true, Toothless has yet to don a Santa hat, but you never know what could be added next year and into the future.

You can check out a video overview of Snoggletog during the daytime via Orlando Informer below:.

A post shared by Orlando Informer (@orlandoinformer).

It has been revealed that I have to say, the thing that most caught my eye was the wreath full of apples. It’s the perfect decor idea that not only looks beautifully festive but would also just be delicious. I also love that you can find a tree made of wood inside Hiccup’s Workshop that you could probably easily replicate if you’re crafty, or you can just pick up themed ornaments for your own home holiday tree.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

If you’re going to be in Orlando in the near future, you can experience Snoggletog at Epic Universe and then head over to the Universal Orlando Resort, where you can have a very merry Grinchmas while also rounding out your theme park trip with what is the best theme park holiday parade through January 3, 2027.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please.
  • The stream indicated off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss.
  • Industry observers note that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that try not to get whole armies of Space Marines pasted against the surfaces of planets thanks to your shoddy tactics, please. So ask the bosses of Total War: Warhammer 40,000, who're keen not to have their training workloads doubled because you're a crap general and have gotten a tight-knit force of uber-tough grunts killed unnecessarily, hope as they watch you play. This and other things have been emphasised by a fresh stream showing off over an hour of campaigning in the strategy warhammerer.

The stream indicated off "an expansion" of the build that devs Creative Assembly let folks like RPS bossman Julian give a go at Gamescom in the summer, via an Ultramarines campaign in a system called Praevoss. Described as a middle-of-the-road option in terms of system size, Praevoss is home to three conquerable planets and a couple of others that aren't suitable for stompy unit hijinks.

Industry observers note that each star system's a "contained campaign", so you hop from one to the next, with certain aspects of your army or skills you've built up carrying over. "First and foremost, we want to represent the scale of the whole galaxy, which is just not possible on a single Total War map," the devs explained. "You'd never be able to engage with it. Part of the point is to break this up a bit and allow us to have some more interesting and more bespoke narratives going on. So each of these star systems has a premise, has a narrative, has a specific setup, a specific start [point], [and] specific victory objectives that you've got to go and do." Creative assembly have also been able to play around a bit more with difficulty as a result of this setup.

As the stream properly got going, the devs focused on chatting about unit specialisation, fleet movement, fleet actions, fleet transportation and Space Marine fleet buildings. Your fleet takes the form of major ships which can be parked above a continent on a planet and offer support via reinforcements and bombardment. As far as the Space Marines specifically go, they're designed to be a small force that's tough to kill, rather than a massive one that's able to recover more quickly and aims to overwhelm with sheer numbers as part of its gameplan.

In a recent development, "Losing a whole army of Space Marines is pretty devastating," the devs noted, as if sensing some blunder I might make far in the future. "That's intentional, as that's a whole Space Marine chapter. Like, losing an army of Space Marines, that's a massive deal for them. It would take them decades to recover from that." At least it looks like I'll not be losing any ships too, since their presence seems limited to providing support to the ground troops, rather than battling each other high above the planets.

As of right now, Total War: Warhammer 40,000 remains without a release date, but can be wishlisted on Steam if you fancy.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rolling dice over Thanksgiving doesn't have to be dull, as these highly recommended board games prove. Want to avoid another family get-together battling over Bond Street in Monopoly? There are five beginner-friendly must-haves I'll always recommend for families, and these up the ante without overcomplicating things.

Sources indicate that actually, these are often called 'gateway' games; they're ideal for newcomers and folks who don't have much experience beyond staples like Clue. Easy to learn but with enough nuance to keep you coming back for more, the five highly recommended board games I've listed below are a step up from old favorites yet don't feel overwhelming. They're not just for beginners, either. Some have reshaped the face of the industry with trend-setting mechanics, and I'd say they deserve a place amongst the very best board games.

Recent findings suggest that looking for something very straightforward? This is where I'd start. As noted in our Carcassonne review, the tile-laying game is "inoffensive family fun with heaps of replayability." Basically, you're building a patchwork kingdom and are trying to claim certain landmarks like cities or roads to earn points. Because you have a limited number of tokens to put on the board (and they stay there until those landmarks are finished), being flexible and knowing when to cut your losses is key.

It has been revealed that if your family isn't up for anything complicated, this is my go-to recommendation. Herd Mentality is an easy-going and thoroughly silly board game about not standing out (which makes it great for those who hate the spotlight). You're all asked a simple question like "what is the best sauce?" and then have to scribble down an answer based on what you think everyone else will say. So long as you're in the majority, you get a point. That makes it a great warmup game or a decent choice if everyone's tired and sluggish after Thanksgiving dinner.

According to recent reports, this may be the ultimate party game for many, but it's also a great choice for family get-togethers; as we say in our five-star Codenames review, it's the "ultimate pick-up-and-play party game." After splitting off into teams, you've got to track down specific words laid out in a grid if you want to win - but the team-member guiding you can only provide a single clue that connects them. It's a lot of fun and real headscratcher for everyone involved.

It has been revealed that want something that's still easy-going but is more advanced? I'll always go to bat for this modern classic. Your aim's to complete train routes across North America for points, but there are limited tracks. That means you'll have to judge where your opponents want to go and cut them off at the pass, or risk having to go the long way around and waste precious time. Like I say in my Ticket to Ride review, it feels like a satisfying puzzle with a layer of strategy underneath it all.

In a recent development, it's not exaggerating to say that this is one of the most influential board games of the past 30 years, and it's had an immense impact on the hobby. This is a very clever strategy game about settling an uninhabited island with multiple ways to win, and while it's the most tactical option on this list, it's arguably the best - part of the reason we gave it such a glowing writeup in our Catan review is that you can keep coming back without having the same outcome.

Want more recommendations? Be sure not to miss our guide to the best family board games.

I've been writing about games in one form or another since 2012, but these days you'll find me managing GamesRadar+'s tabletop gaming and toy coverage (I spend my time here handling everything from board game reviews to the latest Lego news). I've also been obsessed with Warhammer since the 1990s, and love nothing more than running tabletop RPGs like D&D as a Dungeon Master.

Yes, I personally think GTA 6's Ultimate Edition is worth it, but it really depends how excited you are for the game and whether you want to get the most out of it.

All of the additional Mod Shops and Stores exclusive to the Ultimate Edition, along with their unique inventory, means you're really adding a lot of cosmetic and personalisation options to the title with the Ultimate Edition.

If you're not the type of player that plans to dress up Jason and Lucia and fiddle with their vehicles, then you may not find value in this.

But it's worth adding that the Classic Car Collection, which adds collectibles quests involving Wyman, are also exclusive to the Ultimate Edition.

You can still enjoy GTA 6 to its fullest without paying for the Ultimate Edition, but you'll get much more out of the game if you do.

Yes, the Ultimate Edition Upgrade can be purchased from the PS Store at any time for $20.00/£20.00/€20.00 and will automatically add all of the extra content to your game once installed.

You'll need to buy the Ultimate Edition Upgrade if you purchase a physical edition of GTA 6, as this content isn't included with the retail release.

#63146. All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar staff appear in GTA 6 game credits, though some aren't listed as "former employees", curiously

All 34 of the infamously fired Rockstar staff appear in GTA 6 game credits, though some aren't listed as "former employees", curiously

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (490 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Eurogamer

💡 Key Takeaways
  • UPDATE 19TH NOVEMBER: All of the 34 fired Rockstar employees appear in the credits for GTA 6.
  • Also, we couldn't identify six names in the "former employees" section of the credits before because they don't appear there, we now know.
  • ORIGINAL STORY 18TH NOVEMBER: Eurogamer can confirm that at least 28 of the 34 employees fired by Rockstar roughly a year ago - in an action that directly led to the employment tribunal Rockstar is at the moment facing in Scotland - are named in the credits of Grand Theft Auto 6.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATE 19TH NOVEMBER: All of the 34 fired Rockstar employees appear in the credits for GTA 6. We were able to confirm the final few names' existence there after Rockstar posted the full credits online - in searchable form. Before this, the process of cross-checking was intensely laborious: it required watching a scrolling list of names for an hour-and-a-half to see if they appeared.

Also, we couldn't identify six names in the "former employees" section of the credits before because they don't appear there, we now know. These names appear listed under the departments the people worked for, as if they still worked at Rockstar. Why this is, we don't know - perhaps it's something to do with being involved in the employment tribunal or not. We're asking Rockstar for clarification.

ORIGINAL STORY 18TH NOVEMBER: Eurogamer can confirm that at least 28 of the 34 employees fired by Rockstar roughly a year ago - in an action that directly led to the employment tribunal Rockstar is at the moment facing in Scotland - are named in the credits of Grand Theft Auto 6.

According to recent reports, we cross-checked a list of 34 names supplied to us by the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain - the same organisation taking action against Rockstar on behalf of the fired employees. And of those names, we found 28 direct matches in the credits, along with a couple of discrepancies we've since verified, and some close-sounding names we're attempting to clarify. Some names may simply be missing. We won't publish the list for privacy reasons.

A number of those fired employees are seeking compensation for unfair dismissal amid allegations of "union busting", in an employment tribunal that comes to an end today. The delayed climax of the case couldn't be more fateful, aligned as it is with tomorrow's release of GTA 6, and the outcome will be historic either way.

According to recent reports, rockstar recently revealed that more than 4,711 people worked at the firm making GTA 6, employed across 12 offices around the world - a staff-count that has more than doubled since Red Dead Redemption 2. It's a game that's wowed critics - Eurogamer awarded GTA 6 five stars in our review this afternoon - and which observers expect to generate $2bn in revenue in its opening weekend alone.

Recent findings suggest that but perhaps Christian Donlan put it best when digesting the opulence on display in the Netflix 'extended look' GTA 6 trailer. "To spend all this money making something so beautifully rich and detailed, to pay billions for this game and sweat every little animation, to float it out to us on Netflix, amongst genuine discussion around whether Netflix can handle it? That's commitment," he wrote. "And if you're willing to do that, and willing to do that to tell an underdog story, you should let your workers who made everything form a union.".

  • Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap.
  • The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that your next gaming monitor should be an OLED display. There, I've stated it. And I know the notion won't please everyone. After all, a large grey proboscidean lumbers into the room whenever OLED technology is mentioned. Put simply, almost any risk of the dreaded burn-in is an immediate deal-breaker for some. I do get that.

Likewise, despite my musings just the other day on how affordable gaming monitors have generally become and the fact you can now snag an OLED panel, specifically, for sub £300 / $300, it's a stretch to say OLED gaming comes cheap. And yet here I am arguing firmly in favour of OLED.

The point is that OLED is fundamentally superior to LCD, the latter being the dominant display tech on the PC for decades and also, as it happens, an unambiguous technological kludge. Understanding why is the relatively easy bit. Where things get extraordinarily, even belligerently, complicated concerns the current OLED gaming monitor market and the baffling array of panel types and monitor models on offer.

We'll get to all that. But let's start with the core appeal of OLED, which comes down to two factors: lighting control and speed. In both regards, OLED technology completely annihilates LCD. The thing about OLED panels and lighting is that each pixel is its own individually controlled light source. Actually, each subpixel is.

Industry observers note that that means literally perfect lighting control. There's no leakage, no need for bodges like local dimming. Just the ability to have immediately adjacent pixels doing absolutely opposite things, one fully lit up, the other totally off. The impact of that on contrast is epic. In short, if you want a true HDR experience that combines sizzling bright highlights with properly controlled black levels, only OLED can do that.

Sources indicate that the problem with LCD, you see, is that it's a transmissive technology, so light is pushed through the pixels from a big, dumb backlight behind. The liquid crystals in each subpixel are then oriented by an electric charge, controlling the quantity and colour of the light output. In practice, there are oh so many limitations to that approach.

Sources indicate that chief among these problems is that the backlight leaks through in all kinds of unintended ways. And let's be clear, technologies like mini-LED backlights with full-array local dimming don't get anywhere near entirely compensating for LCD's shortcomings. For starters, even a mini-LED backlight with 2,000 zones is very, very low resolution in terms of lighting.

With that kind of zone count, you're looking at a backlight resolution of roughly 55 zones by 35 zones in a 16:9 monitor. Imagine if the actual image resolution was 55 by 35 pixels. Yuck. In the context of a 4K monitor, then, each zone is shared across approximately 4,000 pixels. That's a lot and it translates into visible blooming, weird brightness gradients, dimming zones noticeably popping on and off and all that messy, ugly stuff.

While we're talking liquid crystals twisting in the electrical wind, that's also the reason why LCD is so much slower than OLED. It involves the physical rotation of those rod-shaped crystals to update the image. Like I noted, the pixels in an OLED panel are their own light-emitting diode sources, and very rapidly reacting ones at that. So, OLED response times are essentially instantaneous from a human perception perspective.

I will admit, it's still impressive how good modern LCD panels can look, despite their numerous baked-in limitations. But in lots of important ways, OLED is inherently more suited to gaming displays than LCD. The catch is that it, too, is imperfect, ye olde burn-in being the most obvious shortcoming.

The "O" in OLED refers to "organic", as in Organic Light Emitting Diode. The "organic" bit translates into carbon-based molecules that degrade with use. In short, the harder you drive an OLED pixel, the more its ability to output light is worn out. Over time, the whole panel will wear to some degree, degrading maximum light output. But the real fear is differential wear that leads to unevenness across the screen. The classic scenario is static on-screen interface furniture, perhaps the Windows task bar or persistent parts of a game interface like a health bar or minimap. Eventually, those elements will lead to uneven panel wear.

Pretty much all current OLED gaming monitors have various burn-in mitigation technologies, such as pixel shift, refresh cycles, edge dimming and so on. But none entirely solve the problem. As for real-world expectations of just how bad burn-in can be, there are several independent assessments of OLED monitor burn-in. For instance, Monitors Unboxed has been running one that's now at the 30-month mark, testing absolute worst-case usage on the MSI MPG 321URX, which is from the first generation of 4K, Samsung-made QD-OLED panels.

For what it's worth, my overall view - based on both personal experience with numerous OLED panels over the last few years, and what you might call the emerging consensus - is that burn-in is a real problem, but shouldn't stop most of us buying an OLED. The aforementioned worst-case scenario usage includes driving the panel hard in terms of brightness settings, routine use of persistent interface elements and even failing to allow burn-in mitigation measures to run optimally. Basically, doing all the wrong things. And the evidence is that even this doesn't lead to truly catastrophic burn-in.

After a year of really heavy daily use, you'll probably see some very slight burn-in that's only visible if you go out of your way to look for it. In the second and third years, the burn-in will become more apparent, but only gradually, and even then it will likely still only be visible in certain situations, like an application window with a uniform grey background. The panel will also experience a touch of overall brightness drop off, but not enough to be subjectively noticeable.

Industry observers note that all of that applies to early OLED monitors released three to four years ago, starting with the Alienware 34 AW3423DW. By definition, it hasn't been possible to test recently released panel generations over several years. But each new generation has arrived with promises of improved burn-in resistance.

If that's an overview of generic OLED tech, what about the specifics of the stuff available to buy? It turns out all OLED gaming monitors use panels from just two sources, LG and Samsung. Strictly, there is a new player just arriving on the scene, TCL CSOT, and with it a novel so-called inkjet OLED tech. But there's little to nothing you can actually buy right now with that technology in the gaming space.

According to recent reports, so, LG and Samsung it is. LG's tech has broadly been branded "WOLED", where the "W" stands for "white", while Samsung's panels have been branded "QD-OLED", with the "QD" referring to quantum dot technology. Whether you buy an OLED monitor from Asus, MSI, Alienware or anywhere else, it'll use one of those two basic panel types.

It has been revealed that indeed, until recently, it's been relatively simple to generalise about the two options. LG's WOLED panels used an additional white subpixel to boost peak brightness. Samsung's QD-OLED, meanwhile, had the edge for colour volume and vibrancy, thanks to its strategy of sticking with standard red, green and blue subpixels. Quantum dot tech also more efficiently converts the blue light generated by Samsung's emissive OLED layers into coloured light, compared to the simple filters LG uses to convert white light into coloured light.

Both shared essentially the same near-instantaneous 0.03ms pixel response. Combine that with high refresh rates and the result is razor-sharp motion clarity. However, there were and remain some further detailed differences. Samsung QD-OLED suffered from so-called purple tinting in bright ambient light due to the structure of the panel and the use of quantum dots, which can be activated by ambient light. Basically, stick one of the first three generations of QD-OLED panel next to a window on a bright day and it turns a bit purpley-grey, compromising black levels and overall contrast. On the other hand, the colours in LG's WOLEDs could look a little washed out, due to the use of that white subpixel to boost brightness.

Sources indicate that over those early panel generations, LG also had the edge when it came to image sharpness. Computer OSes like Windows function under the assumption that the subpixels in a digital display are arranged in a vertical RGB-stripe arrangement. LG's "RGWB" stripe, or red, green, white and blue subpixels arranged in vertical stripes, was much closer to that ideal RGB-stripe than Samsung's QD-OLED panels, which had an oddly triangular RGB subpixel structure. The upshot was that those triangular subpixel QD-OLED panels suffered from text fringing and a very slight softness in image quality, comparatively.

In a recent development, however, much of that has changed for the most recent generations of panels released in the last six to 12 months. The hot new thing, at least in terms of branding, is "tandem" OLED technology. Thus, LG has its new "Tandem WOLED" panels and Samsung has "Penta Tandem QD-OLED" tech.

Industry observers note that in both cases, you might imagine the "tandem" bit implies fully dual-layer OLED panels, like those used by Apple in its iPad Pro tablets and the newly introduced PROLED MacBook Pro display. But actually, it refers to added emissive layers within the subpixels. LG's latest panels actually now have four layers, while Samsung's have five, hence the latter's pointed "Penta" branding flex. Either way, the added layers are claimed to increase brightness and improve durability.

Early monitor models based on either OLED panel type (like the aforementioned OG Alienware) tended to top out at around 250 nits of full-screen brightness, which I'd argue wasn't really good enough. The newer "tandem" generations have upped that to 300 and 335 nits for Samsung and LG respectively, which is closing in on the 400 nits I personally think is required to consider the full-screen brightness problem solved. Just note those figures are for pure white brightness, a metric that naturally favours LG's panels with their added white subpixel.

When it comes to colour brightness - and, in practice, most images you look at in-game are coloured, not pure white - Samsung's QD-OLED tech is often brighter. Don't, then, assume a higher outright brightness rating means brighter games. It's more complicated than that. The arrival of the Samsung Penta Tandem QD-OLED generation also brought with it an improvement, but not a total eradication, of the purple-tint glitch in bright ambient light.

Sources indicate that if you've followed all that. and honestly, props if you have, I'm afraid to say this is where things get really baffling. Both LG and Samsung have also released pure RGB-stripe subpixel variants of their newest "tandem" OLED panel tech. For LG, that means dropping the white subpixel for the sake of both better colour volume and more precise rendering, but slightly to the detriment of peak brightness. For Samsung, that means a switch from the triangular subpixel arrangement to vertical RGB-stripe and mostly just an improvement in pixel precision and text quality.

Not all of these panel types are available in all shapes, sizes and resolutions. But it gets confusing really fast. Right now, for instance, there are no fewer than six different 32-inch 4K OLED panel types to choose from. From LG you can have its original RGWB WOLED in, say, the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCDP, the new RGWB Tandem WOLED (for instance, the Asus ROG Strix XG32UQWMS) and then finally the RGB-stripe variation on Tandem WOLED ( see the Asus ROG Swift PG32UCWM). From Samsung, meanwhile, you can choose between its original triangular subpixel QD-OLED (like on the MSI MAG 321UP), the Penta Tandem follow up (of the MSI MPG 321UP X24) and then the all-singing RGB-stripe Penta Tandem (of the MSI MPG OLED 322URDX36, which is just about to be released).

Just to complicate things even further, LG's RGB-stripe "tandem" panels are still branded "WOLED", because the "W" in WOLED doesn't and has never referred to the white subpixels LG had hitherto used, but instead the white colour of the light produced by the emissive layers within each subpixel before conversion by the RGB filters. Got that? Phew.

In a recent development, the long and short of all this is that if you're comparing the very latest "tandem RGB-stripe" panels from LG and Samsung, they are closer now in terms of the subjective experience than ever before. Up until this generation, I always favoured QD-OLED for its superior colour vibrancy while accepting the purple tint matter. But as I peck out these words on the latest 39-inch 5K2K Alienware AW3926QW and its Tandem WOLED RGB-stripe panel, I think I might just lean LG right now for its superior contrast in bright ambient light conditions, as well as this slightly more neutral subjective colour balance.

Anyway, as much as all that may feel like an exhaustive (and exhausting) dissertation, there is actually a fair bit I don't have space to fully cover. There are slight variations in the panel types, for instance, in terms of issues like uniformity and graininess, colour shift as opposed to outright burn-in, and also OLED flicker. But I wouldn't consider any of those even near to being deal breakers.

Really, it's just the long-term outlook that would have me thinking twice. First, that involves burn-in. I'd be pretty confident of getting at least three years out of an OLED. The significant brands all have three year burn-in cover in any case (which is a very good reason to favour a big, familiar brand that you can be fairly certain will honour that warranty down the road). And it wouldn't surprise me if five years was very doable with the latest panels. The catch is that you can't, currently, be entirely sure about that.

Industry observers note that second, OLED technology is developing fast. It's come a long way in the last few years and I suspect that the next few will see comparable progress. Two or three years from now, I think full-screen brightness will likely be a totally solved problem, for instance, burn-in will be barely any concern at all, and prices will have come down even further. Ultimately, however, I wouldn't let that expectation stop me buying an OLED. It may not be entirely without flaws. But OLED is still by far the best PC display tech available today.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We got our first technical deep dive into AMD's next-generation Zen 6 CPU architecture last week, in the form of the firm's newly introduced Venice range of server chips. Now there's a rumour that the consumer Ryzen chip launch may have been pushed back to the second half of 2027.

Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced Ryzen offerings were originally thought to be launching in the first half, but Chiphell leaker Zhang Zhonghao claims otherwise. In a post spotted by Videocardz, Zhang Zhonghao claims that the desktop chips, codenamed Olympic Ridge, have been switched to TSMC's N2X manufacturing process, and as a result the "timeline has been pushed back" (via machine translation).

Zhang Zhonghao makes mention of Computex in their post, which some are speculating means a launch date after the show in June of next year.

Olympic Ridge was originally though to be using TSMC's N2 or N2P process node, but a switch to the performance-focussed N2X would line up with previous rumours that the chips are targeting very high clockspeeds, potentially all the way up to 6.5 GHz.

According to recent reports, N2X is scheduled to enter production in 2027, which would explain the longer timeframe if this rumour proves out. A delay to the second half of next year would mean that Intel's Nova Lake chips, remarked by the company to be "tracking ahead of schedule" in a recent earnings call, would potentially have the first half of 2026 all to themselves if they launch before Zen 6.

It has been revealed that in the battle of the next generation CPUs, Intel would end up with a significant headstart. However, for those thinking about a potential upgrade, it's worth noting that Intel's latest chips will use an entirely new socket in the form of LGA 1954. AMD's new offerings will use the existing AM5 socket.

AMD's Jack Huynh posted a cryptic video on X earlier this week, alongside a message declaring that "the next era of computing is going to be special," and that he "can't wait to share a glimpse of what's coming at CES." So, hopefully we might learn more about what's going on with Zen 6 desktop silicon on January 5.

First-person psychological horror game BrokenLore: MIKI-CHAN will launch for Switch 2 alongside its previously unveiled PlayStation 5, Xbox Series, and PC (Steam, Epic Games Store) versions in 2027, Serafini Productions announced.

Here is an overview of the game, via Serafini Productions:.

BrokenLore: MIKI-CHAN is a first-person psychological horror game that follows Kazuaki, a Japanese student determined to pass the entrance exam for Teidai and win over the girl he loves.

When he finds a mysterious USB stick containing an innovative study support program, he decides to try it, convinced that it can help him.

Waiting for him is Miki-chan, a sweet and reassuring virtual assistant. But something soon changes. Jealousy and possessiveness take over, dragging Kazuaki into a nightmare.

Kazuaki will face psychological challenges that push him to his limits. But he has the Rewriter at his disposal, a tool capable of altering reality.

Sources indicate that universal Epic Universe is currently celebrating its second holiday season with more holiday decorations than last year and a upcoming Dark Universe ride currently under construction. There’s even more gifts from the theme park during this time of merriment! It’s just been declared that for the first time ever Epic is going to be added into the Annual Pass mix. The news led to a mix of huge excitement and tons of questions.

In a Universal Parks announcement, the Orlando resort shared that annual passes featuring Universal Epic Universe access are coming in early December. Guests with current annual passes will be able to upgrade their current passes, and those looking to purchase one can do so at this time. Unlike the other parks, there will be a reservation system in place with the earliest date to go with a pass being January 4, 2027. Check out some of the spirited reactions from Twitter:.

Recent findings suggest that ever since Epic Universe opened its gates in May of last year, it has quickly become a favorite park with tons of great rides to check out. For those who want to return there again and again (and perhaps make time to notice the park’s fun easter eggs) an annual pass is always a great value. Fans are rightfully hyped.

Whenever there’s a substantial change at one of Universal Orlando’s parks, inquiries typically follow, and there’s a lot popping up amidst the announcement. Here’s a few big ones:.

In a recent development, universal was all over the comment section trying to answer some of these questions. Most of them seem to point to there being another wave of details on the way, but for now Universal Orlando’s Annual Pass website has been refreshed with current steps to take if you'd like to upgrade.

According to recent reports, universal Orlando Resort will still offer four different types of pass tiers, but the announcement includes a complete re-branding of the system. Those who hold these memberships will be called “Pass Members” rather than “Passholders” and the type names will go from being called Seasonal, Power, Preferred and Premier to Bronze, Silver, Gold and Platinum. They’re also going completely digital with all physical passes being phased out over time.

Sources indicate that in regards to the Epic Universe upgrade, current Passholders will be given a timeframe for when they can upgrade their passes, and current holders will be able to switch before anyone else. Those who are in their renewal period will also have the option to “pay a price difference of $125 to $410 to renew into a Pass with Universal Epic Universe access, depending on Pass type.” Annual passes right now cost between $475 and $1015, based on that price difference info; the price range might have changed to between $600 to $1425, but all the details are not yet clear to anyone quite yet.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Universal is already teasing more information on the way “soon." Either way, it’s quite exciting that those interested will soon get to enjoy Epic Universe over and over.

PSA: Some GTA 6 Ultimate Edition content is only available for the first chapter, and you'll have to put in hard graft to unlock more

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that GTA 6's Ultimate Edition has proven enormously popular, despite its hefty $100 price tag.
  • As previously confirmed, the $100/£90 Ultimate Edition provides access to exclusive vehicles, weapons, shops, and more, with the full list as follows:.
  • Rockstar also previously revealed that "Ultimate Edition bonuses become available to Jason and Lucia across their story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that GTA 6's Ultimate Edition has proven enormously popular, despite its hefty $100 price tag. So much so that Strauss Zelnick, boss of Rockstar parent organization Take-Two, recently confirmed it's the edition most people are buying - and that's despite a lack of specific information about how its unlockable content works. With GTA 6 just hours away from release, however - and out now in certain parts of the work - details are beginning to emerge, and the answer is perhaps a little surprising.

As previously confirmed, the $100/£90 Ultimate Edition provides access to exclusive vehicles, weapons, shops, and more, with the full list as follows:.

Rockstar also previously revealed that "Ultimate Edition bonuses become available to Jason and Lucia across their story, with new items uncovered behind each chapter". The specifics of how - and when - all this stuff unlocks, though, remained unclear. So if you've opted for the Ultimate Edition, you might be wondering where your stuff is when you finally fire up the game. As reported by IGN, which has full unlock details, it turns out virtually all of GTA 6's Ultimate Edition content, as per details in the in-game shop, requires progressing through the main story - in some cases dozens and dozens of hours into the story - before it'll become available.

Recent findings suggest that ultimate Edition-exclusive shops, for instance, unlock during Chapter 1, and many of the other additions become available by the end of Chapter 2. That doesn't sound too difficult, but as Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell notes, reaching that point could take upward of 25 hours. As for some of the late-game unlocks, such as the Shitzu Squalo and the Vice City Style outfits and tattoos (available in Chapter 4) and Chapter 5's 95 Grotti Cheetah, you could be looking at closing in on 60 hours of playtime before they unlock.

"It'll vary depending how hard people focus on the main story," Chris explains, "but if you were mostly focused on the main story plus the optional character-based missions in largely chronological order, that's about how long it'd take.".

Sources indicate that it's also worth noting - perhaps surprisingly - that some Ultimate Edition content is only a temporary unlock, usable only during specific chapters. Jason's Dinka Enduro motorcycle and Crest Kayak, for instance, can only be accessed and enjoyed during Chapter 1. That's also true for his retro Vapid Ganado, available from the Coastal Auto Care mod shop in Key Lento. So basically, you'll want to make the most of these while you can!

Recent findings suggest that all this might be a little disappointing for players who were expecting to be showered with Ultimate Edition spoils from the off (and that they'd be permanent unlocks), but the good news is 60 hours in GTA 6 is far from a chore. As Chris explained in his five star GTA 6 review, Rockstar's latest is an "irreducible mix of silliness, intimacy, grand ideas and rock 'n' roll action" that "pushes back the horizon of video games once again".
